value.overview: The Yellow-headed Caracara is a medium-sized, adaptable raptor of the falcon family. It is recognizable by its pale yellow head and underparts, dark brown back and wings, and long tail. Unlike many birds of prey, it often walks on the ground while searching for food. It uses open landscapes, forest edges, wetlands, pastures, and agricultural areas, where it scavenges, hunts small animals, and takes advantage of many human-altered habitats.
value.classification: The Yellow-headed Caracara belongs to the family Falconidae, which includes falcons, caracaras, and forest falcons. Its accepted scientific name is Daptrius chimachima; older sources commonly use Milvago chimachima.
value.identification: This caracara has a pale buff-yellow head, neck, breast, and belly, usually with fine darker streaking on the head and throat. The back, wings, and upper tail are dark brown, while the lower back and rump are pale or whitish. The tail is barred, and the bill and legs are bluish gray. It has a relatively small crest compared with the Crested Caracara. Its upright posture, broad wings, and habit of walking through grass help identify it.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Costa Rica through much of tropical South America to northern Argentina and Uruguay. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in the warmer Pacific lowlands and other open or semi-open areas, including pastures, cultivated land, savannas, wetlands, mangroves, forest edges, and clearings. It may also appear around roads, ranches, and settlements. It generally avoids extensive, closed-canopy interior forest, although it can use forest margins and openings.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range. It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant, although local movements and dispersal may occur in response to food, weather, or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The Yellow-headed Caracara usually nests in trees, often selecting a palm or another tall tree in open country, forest edge, or a wetland margin. The nest is a bulky platform made from sticks and may be reused or repaired. The species can breed during much of the year in tropical regions. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported year-round, with activity varying by locality and often increasing during the dry season and early rainy season. Both adults participate in raising the young.
value.dietFeeding: It is an opportunistic feeder that takes carrion, insects, small reptiles, amphibians, fish, crabs, nestlings, eggs, and other small animals. It may follow livestock, search along roadsides, probe soil and leaf litter, or inspect shallow water and mud. It sometimes takes food from larger predators or scavengers. Its broad diet and willingness to forage on the ground allow it to thrive in pastures, farms, wetlands, and other modified landscapes.
value.behavior: This caracara is often seen alone, in pairs, or in small loose groups. It spends considerable time perched on poles, fence posts, dead branches, and palms, but frequently descends to walk across the ground. It is an alert and active scavenger, often investigating disturbances, livestock areas, and exposed carrion. Its flight consists of steady wingbeats mixed with gliding, and it may soar while searching for food or defending a territory.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable overall, although local numbers may vary with land-use change, food availability, persecution, and other regional pressures.
